kurals.tamil:
உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம் அஃதில்லார்
உடையது உடையரோ மற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Udaiyar enappaduvadhu ookkam aqdhillaar
Udaiyadhu udaiyaro matru.
kurals.meaning: The only thing that truly makes a person an owner is inner energy; those without it do not really possess anything, whatever else they may hold.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two children who are each given a box of paints. One gets excited and paints every day; the other leaves the box closed on a shelf. Only the first one really ‘has’ paints. The Kural says the eager, energetic spirit is the thing that makes anything you own actually yours.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by redefining possession itself: “udaiyar enappaduvadhu” (what it is to be called a possessor) is ookkam, which Parimelazhagar glosses as mental elation or upsurge of the will toward action (ullaezhuchi), the drive that animates effort rather than effort itself. The rhetorical question “udaiyadhu udaiyaro” (do they own what they own?) denies that the unenergetic possess even their existing wealth, since without ookkam it will neither be defended nor increased; “matru” is treated by the commentators as an expletive particle (asai). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all paraphrase the line as ‘only the energetic are truly possessors’, and the text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The adhikaram sits in Arasiyal (royalty), after Espionage and before Unsluggishness (Madiyinmai), Manly Effort (Aalvinaiyudaimai) and Not Despairing in Trouble, forming a cluster on the psychology of exertion that parallels the Sanskrit utsāha-śakti, the ‘power of energy’ that Kautilya lists among a king’s three powers. Thirukkural.net titles the chapter ‘Magnanimity’, while Pope and ytamizh.com use ‘Energy’, reflecting the double sense of ookkam as both drive and largeness of spirit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The performer is said to be in the mode of goodness, when he or she is free from egotism and attachment, endowed with enthusiasm and determination, and equipoised in success and failure.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the best kind of worker as one filled with utsāha (zeal) and dhṛti (resolve), who keeps working steadily whatever the outcome.
hinduism.tie_back: Utsāha is the Sanskrit counterpart of ookkam, and the Gita, like the Kural, makes it a defining trait of the worthy person.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct terminological match (utsāha = ookkam), though the Gita frames zeal within detachment rather than as the essence of ownership.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to put their whole heart and energy into every task, treating even ordinary work as service to God.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat wholehearted inner energy as what gives a person’s life and work its real value.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the ideal of wholehearted zeal, but Paul’s motive is devotion to God, not the Kural’s claim that energy is the only true possession.

islam.quote_or_event: “A strong believer is better and is more lovable to Allah than a weak believer, and there is good in everyone, (but) cherish that which gives you benefit (in the Hereafter) and seek help from Allah and do not lose heart…”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises the strong, active believer and tells people to pursue what benefits them eagerly and never give in to helplessness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ookkam and the hadith’s strength and refusal of ‘ajz (helplessness) both mark the energetic person as the one of real worth.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; the hadith joins energy to reliance on God, which the Kural does not mention.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whatsoever thy hand attaineth to do by thy strength, that do; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth urges people to act with all their strength now, because this life is the only arena for effort.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that the energy you bring to action is what counts, more than anything you merely hold.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong call to energetic action; its motive is life’s brevity rather than the Kural’s theory of what counts as ownership.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kasibharadvaja Sutta the Buddha answers a ploughing brahmin by describing his own ‘farming’, in which faith is the seed and energy (viriya) is the draught-ox that carries him forward to freedom from bondage.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells a farmer that his spiritual work has its own plough and oxen, and energy is the beast that pulls everything forward.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, energy is the working asset that makes every other endowment productive.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; viriya as the driving force is a good match, though the sutta’s goal is liberation rather than worldly possession.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, born with divine strength, wins his lasting fame only through the Twelve Labours, a lifetime of relentless exertion undertaken at Eurystheus’ command.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles’ gifts meant little until he threw himself into one exhausting task after another, and his tireless striving is what made him a hero.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth illustrates the Kural’s point that endowment without energetic use is not true possession.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An illustrative parallel only; the myth celebrates endurance and heroism rather than stating a doctrine about ownership.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that happiness lies in virtuous activity, not in merely having a good disposition: just as at the Olympic Games it is not the finest and strongest who are crowned but those who actually compete, so in life those who act rightly win the prize.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle a capacity you never use is like a strong athlete who never enters the race; only active exercise (energeia) earns the good.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says that what you hold counts only if energy puts it to work.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close conceptual parallel between energeia and ookkam as activity over mere possession.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளம் உடைமை உடைமை பொருளுடைமை
நில்லாது நீங்கி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullam udaimai udaimai poruludaimai
Nillaadhu neengi vidum.
kurals.meaning: Energy of mind is the possession that lasts; material wealth does not stay but slips away.
kurals.elementary: A sandcastle can be washed away by the next wave, but the skill and excitement that built it stay with you, so you can build another one tomorrow. Money and things can disappear, but a strong, eager mind stays yours.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two kinds of udaimai (property) against each other: ullam udaimai, possession of ‘mind’, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss as ookkam, and porul udaimai, possession of goods. The triple repetition ‘udaimai udaimai … udaimai’ is a deliberate sound-play (sol-pin-varunilai) that forces the reader to ask which ‘having’ deserves the name. The verbs ‘nillaadhu neengi vidum’ (does not stay, departs) echo the Aram-section chapter on impermanence (Nilaiyaamai, ch. 34), but here the lesson is practical rather than renunciatory: since wealth is fugitive, the ruler’s real capital is the energy that can regain it. Solomon Pappaiah renders ullam as mana uruthi (firmness of mind), a slight shift from zeal to resolve. The text agrees verbatim in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Yama offers Nachiketas cattle, gold, horses and long-lived sons in place of the secret of death, the boy refuses, answering that a man cannot be satisfied by wealth and that such things wear away the vigour of the senses.
hinduism.explanation: Nachiketas turns down every treasure Death offers because riches are temporary and cannot give lasting satisfaction.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Upanishad ranks an inner possession above material goods that ‘do not stay’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the contrast between fleeting wealth and inner worth, but the inner treasure is self-knowledge rather than energy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that earthly riches decay or are stolen, and urges people to invest in the lasting treasure of the spirit.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same contrast between perishable wealth and an inner possession that abides.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel; the lasting treasure is heavenly merit, not the Kural’s energy of mind.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth is not in having many possessions, but rather (true) wealth is feeling sufficiency in the soul.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that true richness is an inner state of the soul, not a large pile of goods.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings redefine real wealth as something held within the self.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close in form; the inner wealth is contentment rather than energy, which is a real difference of emphasis.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot…”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines riches as an inner disposition toward one’s portion, not the size of one’s holdings.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mishnah locates true possession in the mind rather than in property.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same move of relocating wealth inward, but the inner quality is contentment, not zeal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists seven ‘noble treasures’ (faith, virtue, conscience, concern, learning, generosity and discernment) and says that, unlike gold, they cannot be taken by kings, thieves, fire or flood.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts qualities of mind that no disaster can seize with material riches that can be lost at any time.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too says wealth ‘departs’ while a possession of the mind remains.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; an excellent structural match, though energy (viriya) is not among the seven treasures listed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas is granted the golden touch, but his food and drink turn to gold, and he begs Dionysus to take the gift away, washing it off in the river Pactolus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas learns that a mountain of gold is worthless and even harmful when it cannot sustain life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The story shows the Kural’s point that material wealth is not a true or lasting possession.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shows the hollowness of wealth but offers no positive counterpart like ookkam.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy tells the imprisoned Boethius that Fortune’s gifts of wealth and rank were never truly his, since what can be taken away does not belong to a person; only goods of the mind are one’s own.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius, stripped of wealth and office, is taught that external goods are only on loan from Fortune.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s claim that property ‘does not stay but departs’ while the mind’s possession endures.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong parallel on fleeting external goods, though Boethius’ inner good is reason and virtue rather than energy.

kurals.tamil:
ஆக்கம் இழந்தேமென்று அல்லாவார் ஊக்கம்
ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடை யார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aakkam izhandhemendru allaavaar ookkam
Oruvandham kaiththudai yaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who firmly hold energy in their hands do not grieve, saying ‘we have lost our wealth’.
kurals.elementary: If a strong wind knocks down your block tower, you can cry about it, or you can say ‘I still have my hands and my ideas’ and build again. People with real energy don’t sit around moaning about what they lost; they know they can make more.
kurals.university: The key image is ‘kaiththu udaiyaar’: those who hold ookkam as kaipporul, ready money in the hand, which Parimelazhagar reads as the secure capital that makes lost aakkam (prosperity) recoverable. ‘Oruvandham’ means certainly or firmly (nichchayamaaga), qualifying the grip on energy; ‘allaavaar’ (will not be distressed) derives from allal, affliction. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the implied condition ‘even when prosperity has actually been lost’, while Kalaignar stresses that such people do not lose their ookkam along with their wealth. The couplet thus answers 592: if wealth departs, energy remains the seed of its return, which is why the chapter treats ookkam as a king’s fundamental resource. The Tamil text is identical in both base sources, differing only in word-splitting (izhandhemendru vs. izhandhaem endru).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One whose mind remains undisturbed amidst misery, who does not crave for pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady-minded person who does not fall apart when troubles come.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s energetic person, like the Gita’s sthita-prajña, is not shaken into lament by loss.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the refusal to be distressed by misfortune; the Gita grounds it in detachment, the Kural in confident energy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned to stay steady whether he has plenty or nothing.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s energetic person, Paul does not collapse into complaint when his resources vanish.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on equanimity in loss; Paul’s strength comes from Christ (4:13) rather than native energy.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches believers not to be crushed by what they have lost nor puffed up by what they have gained.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the strong-spirited do not lament lost prosperity.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on not grieving over loss; the Qur’anic ground is trust in divine decree rather than self-possessed energy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, And naked shall I return thither; The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; Blessed be the name of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: Having lost his flocks, servants and children in one day, Job refuses to curse or despair.
judaism.tie_back: Job embodies the Kural’s refusal to cry ‘we have lost our wealth’, though from faith rather than energy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong example of not lamenting loss; the motive is submission to God, not confidence in one’s own power to recover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures the wise as a rock that stays put whatever storms of fortune blow against it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s energetic person is similarly unshaken by the storm of lost prosperity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Captures steadiness under changing fortune, but concerns praise and blame rather than loss of wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus loses every ship, every companion and all his Trojan treasure, yet he washes up naked on Scheria and still presses on until he regains his home and kingdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: Stripped of everything, Odysseus keeps his resourceful, tireless spirit and uses it to win back all he had.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He shows the Kural’s idea that energy held ‘in hand’ outlasts lost wealth and can restore it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A vivid narrative match for recovering from total loss by inner resource.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells how Stilpo, whose city had been captured and his family and property lost, was asked by Demetrius whether he had lost anything, and replied that he had lost nothing, for all his goods were with him.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher Stilpo insists that real goods live inside a person and cannot be plundered.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ookkam-holder, Stilpo does not say ‘I have lost my wealth’ because his real capital is within.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a near-exact situational parallel, though Stilpo’s inner good is wisdom rather than energy.

kurals.tamil:
ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா
ஊக்க முடையா னுழை.
kurals.transliteration:
Aakkam adharvinaaich chellum asaivilaa
Ookkam udaiyaan uzhai.
kurals.meaning: Prosperity itself asks the way and travels to the home of the person whose energy never wavers.
kurals.elementary: Picture good luck as a little traveller with a map, going around asking, ‘Where does the hardworking kid live?’ The Kural says success goes looking for people who never give up.
kurals.university: Valluvar personifies aakkam (prosperity, increase) as a traveller who ‘adhar vinaai’, asks the road (adhar = path), to reach the dwelling (uzhai) of the man of unwavering (asaivilaa) energy. Parimelazhagar notes that prosperity need not be sought by such a person; it seeks him, a reversal of the usual image of the striver chasing fortune. Solomon Pappaiah’s modern rendering, ‘wealth learns his address and goes to him’, keeps the playful personification. The idea closely matches the Sanskrit subhāṣita ‘udyoginaṁ puruṣa-siṁham upaiti lakṣmīḥ’ (Lakshmi approaches the lion-like man of effort), found in the Hitopadesha prologue, showing a shared Indian topos. The two base sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net joins ‘ookka mudaiyaa nuzhai’ as in the metrical manuscripts, which is simply the sandhi form of ‘ookkam udaiyaan uzhai’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, approaches the lion-like man of effort; only cowards say that fortune is simply handed out by fate, so set fate aside and exert yourself with your own strength.
hinduism.explanation: The Hitopadesha’s famous verse says prosperity comes to the energetic, not to those who wait on destiny.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own image: fortune travels to the unwavering man of energy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the Sanskrit; a near one-to-one match of the idea that fortune seeks out the energetic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servants who actively traded with their money are given far more, while the one who buried his talent loses it.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, increase flows to the one who acts energetically with what he has.
christianity._accuracy_note: The parable rewards active diligence, though its reward is the master’s gift and its meaning is spiritual stewardship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an states that what a person gains corresponds to the effort he puts in.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly ties prosperity to unwavering effort.
islam._accuracy_note: Links reward to striving; the verse concerns moral recompense before God more than worldly prosperity.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs teaches that the one who works with a slack hand becomes poor, while the hand of the diligent brings riches.
judaism.explanation: The sages of Proverbs connect wealth directly to diligent, energetic effort and poverty to slackness.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the same, adding the image of prosperity actively seeking out the diligent.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a direct thematic match on diligence producing wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that the energetic, careful person steadily grows in honour and standing.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises increase to the one whose energy does not flag.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match: energy (uṭṭhāna) brings growing glory, though paired with ethical qualities.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells his brother Perses that the gods have set sweat before excellence, that work is no disgrace, and that if he works the idle will soon envy him as he grows rich, for fame and renown attend on wealth.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s farming poem teaches that prosperity and honour follow the hardworking person.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s promise that prosperity comes to the one of unfailing energy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong thematic match on labour attracting wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy Phormio, a character declares that fortune helps the brave (fortes fortuna adiuvat), a proverb later repeated by Pliny and Cicero.
philosophy.explanation: The Latin proverb says good fortune sides with the bold and energetic.
philosophy.tie_back: It is a Roman version of the Kural’s image of fortune seeking out the unwavering.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A proverb rather than a philosophical argument; courage and energy overlap but are not identical.

kurals.tamil:
வெள்ளத் தனைய மலர்நீட்டம் மாந்தர்தம்
உள்ளத் தனையது உயர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Vellath thanaiya malarneettam maandhardham
Ullath thanaiyadhu uyarvu.
kurals.meaning: Just as a water-flower’s stalk grows as tall as the water is deep, a person rises only as high as the energy of their mind.
kurals.elementary: A lotus in a pond always grows its stem long enough to reach the top of the water. If the pond is deep, the stem is long. The Kural says people are like that: the bigger your spirit and effort, the higher you rise.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s most celebrated image. ‘Vellaththanaiya malar neettam’ means the length of the flower (its stalk) is proportionate to the flood or water-depth; ‘ullaththanaiyadhu uyarvu’ means human height or eminence is proportionate to ullam, which the commentators again take as ookkam. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah speak generally of neerppookkal (water-flowers), while Kalaignar specifies the lotus stalk (thaamarai thandu); the botanical observation that lotus and water-lily stems lengthen to keep the bloom at the surface underlies the comparison. The parallel structure ‘-aththanaiya … -aththanaiyadhu’ is an example of Valluvar’s use of exact grammatical symmetry (ethirnirai) to make the analogy feel like a law. The couplet implies both limit and possibility: stature cannot exceed inner energy, but greater energy raises it. Text identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna urges Arjuna to lift himself up by his own mind and never let himself sink, since the mind can be the self’s best friend or its worst enemy.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita teaches that how high or low a person goes depends on the state of their own mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s lotus image says the same: a person’s height matches the level of their inner energy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong match on self-elevation through the mind, though the Gita’s aim is spiritual rather than worldly eminence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he:”
christianity.explanation: This proverb, often quoted in Christian teaching, says a person’s true character follows what is in their heart and mind.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures a person by the level of their inner life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Popular reading fits well, but in context the verse describes a stingy host’s hidden thoughts, so the match is looser than it appears.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an ties a people’s outward condition to the state of their inner selves.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too makes outer elevation depend on the inner ‘water-level’ of the mind.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong structural match between inner state and outer condition, framed within divine agency.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides teaches that every person has the power to become as righteous as Moses or as wicked as Jeroboam; no decree fixes one’s level, which depends on one’s own choice and effort.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides insists that a person’s spiritual height is not predetermined but set by their own will.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural similarly makes a person’s ‘height’ a function of their own inner resolve.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 5:2
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; parallel on self-determined stature, though focused on moral free will rather than energy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says energy and discipline raise a person above the floodwaters of life.
buddhism.tie_back: Both use water imagery: inner effort determines how far a person rises above the flood.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Effective water-and-effort parallel, though the island image differs from the Kural’s proportional lotus.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar advises his patron Hieron to become such as he is, having learned what that is, urging him to rise to the full measure of his own nature.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet tells a king to grow into the full size of the self he truly has.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the lotus rising to the water-line, Pindar’s ideal is to rise exactly to one’s inner measure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Greek lyric rather than myth, and the maxim’s meaning is debated; offered as the best available analogue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… it makes a material for itself out of that which opposes it, as fire lays hold of what falls into it, by which a small light would have been extinguished: but when the fire is strong, it soon appropriates to itself the matter which is heaped on it, and consumes it, and rises higher by means of this very material.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus says the ruling part of the mind, when it follows nature, turns every obstacle into fuel, as a strong fire feeds on what would smother a weak one.
philosophy.tie_back: Both use an image from nature in which the strength of the inner force decides how high one rises: the stalk with the water, the flame with its own strength.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, §1 (tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long). Partial match: Marcus's point is the mind's power to use adversity, whereas the Kural says one's height matches one's energy of mind; the overlap is the image of inner strength determining how high one rises.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளுவ தெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல் மற்றது
தள்ளினுந் தள்ளாமை நீர்த்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulluva thellaam uyarvullal matradhu
Thallinum thallaamai neerththu.
kurals.meaning: Let every thought be a thought of rising higher; even if fate pushes that aim aside, it has the worth of never having been pushed aside.
kurals.elementary: If you aim to jump over a tall bar and only get halfway, you still jumped higher than if you’d aimed low. The Kural says always think big; even when you don’t reach it, the aiming itself counts.
kurals.university: The first line is a direct precept: ‘ulluvadhellaam uyarvu ullal’, let all that you think be the thinking of elevation. The second line is compressed and has produced different readings. Parimelazhagar (reflected in Pope’s ‘if it should be thrust from him by fate, it will have the nature of not being thrust from him’) takes ‘matradhu thallinum’ as ‘even if that (aim) is thwarted by fate (ool)’ and ‘thallaamai neerththu’ as ‘it has the nature (neermai) of not being thwarted’, since the nobility of the aim remains. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the line as an imperative, ‘do not abandon such thinking even if it fails’, while Solomon Pappaiah adds that the great will praise the attempt, so it counts as fulfilled. Thirukkural.net compresses this as ‘failure then is as good as success’. The text is identical in the base sources; the interpretive variation lies in whether ‘thallaamai’ is descriptive or prescriptive.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s task is the effort itself, not control of outcomes, and that giving up action is never right.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the lofty aim keeps its worth even when fate blocks the result.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the second line’s independence from results, though the Gita does not stress ‘aiming high’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul admits he has not yet arrived but keeps straining forward toward the highest goal.
christianity.tie_back: His constant reaching for the ‘high calling’ is the Kural’s ‘let every thought be of rising’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on perpetual high aspiration despite incompleteness; Paul’s goal is spiritual.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith reported by al-Tabarani and others says that Allah loves lofty and noble matters and dislikes base and petty ones.
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that believers should set their sights on noble, elevated aims rather than trivial ones.
islam.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s command to let every thought be a thought of elevation.
islam.source: al-Tabarani, al-Mu‘jam al-Kabir (hadith on ma‘ali al-umur)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; thematic match on lofty aims, but the exact wording and grading could not be verified against a primary edition.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it;”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Tarfon teaches that one must keep striving at a great task even if it cannot be completed in one’s lifetime.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it values the pursuit of a high aim even when completion is blocked.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel to the second line; Tarfon speaks of Torah study rather than personal eminence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha recalls resolving before his awakening that he would gladly let his flesh and blood dry up, leaving skin, sinews and bones, rather than relax his energy before reaching what can be reached by human strength and effort.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha aimed at the highest goal and vowed never to lower his effort short of it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘think only of rising’, carried to its utmost.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong match on relentless high aspiration, though it does not address failure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles is approached by Vice, offering an easy, pleasant road, and Virtue, offering a steep, hard road to true glory; he chooses the harder, higher path.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles deliberately picks the difficult road that leads upward rather than the comfortable one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His choice embodies the Kural’s rule that one’s aims should always point toward elevation.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good allegory of choosing the high path, but silent on what happens when the aim is thwarted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca defends philosophers who fall short of their ideals, saying one should admire those who attempt great things even when they fail, because the attempt itself is noble.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that striving toward a lofty goal deserves honour even without full success.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s second line: a high aim that is thwarted is as good as one achieved.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On the Happy Life (De Vita Beata) 20
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close match to both lines of the couplet.

kurals.tamil:
சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார் உரவோர் புதையம்பிற்
பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Sidhaividaththu olkaar uravor pudhaiyambir
Pattuppaadu oondrum kaliru.
kurals.meaning: The strong-minded do not falter even in ruin, just as a war elephant, pierced deep by arrows, stands firm and keeps its dignity.
kurals.elementary: Think of a brave firefighter who keeps going even when they are tired and hurt. The Kural compares strong-hearted people to a huge elephant that stays standing even when arrows hit it. Tough times don’t make them quit.
kurals.university: ‘Sidhaividaththu’ means at the place or time of ruin (sidhaivu), and ‘olkaar’ means they do not bend or droop; ‘uravor’ are those with uram, firmness of mind. The simile is from war: ‘pudhai ambu’ are arrows buried in the flesh, and ‘pattup paadu oondrum kaliru’ is the bull elephant that, though struck, plants itself (oondrum) and upholds its paadu, glossed by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as its perumai (greatness, dignity). The image comes from Sangam battle poetry, where the wounded tusker holding its ground is a stock emblem of valour. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘pudhai’ as arrows that cover the body. The spelling ‘kaliru’ (களிறு) is the standard word for a male elephant; the texts in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhishma, pierced by so many of Arjuna’s arrows that when he falls from his chariot his body does not touch the ground, lies on a bed of arrows for many days, calm and lucid, and teaches the Pandavas until his chosen time of death.
hinduism.explanation: The great warrior, riddled with arrows, keeps his composure and his dignity and continues to act as a teacher.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the human counterpart of the Kural’s elephant that stands firm though pierced by arrows.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva (fall of Bhishma), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking image-level parallel of arrows and unbroken dignity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes suffering attacks from every side without being crushed in spirit.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s strong-minded, he is struck but does not falter.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in structure; Paul attributes his endurance to divine power.

islam.quote_or_event: “So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers.”
islam.explanation: After the setback at Uhud, the Qur’an tells the wounded believers not to lose heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too says the strong do not droop even in the hour of ruin.
islam._accuracy_note: Revealed after a military defeat, so the battlefield context aligns well with the elephant image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”
judaism.explanation: God tells Joshua, facing hard battles, to stay strong and not be shaken.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same firmness in danger the Kural praises.
judaism._accuracy_note: An exhortation before trouble rather than endurance amid ruin; grounded in God’s presence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his patient endurance of insults to a war elephant standing firm under a hail of arrows.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use the identical image of the arrow-struck war elephant that does not give way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-identical imagery; the Buddha applies it to verbal abuse rather than ruin in general.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As the Trojans storm the Greek ships, Ajax is battered by missiles until his shoulder aches under his shield and he can barely breathe, yet he keeps his position and does not give ground.
greek_mythology.explanation: The great Greek defender stays at his post even while being hammered from all sides.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ajax holding firm under the barrage mirrors the elephant standing fast though pierced by arrows.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; close battlefield parallel of endurance under a shower of weapons.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like the headland against which the waves keep breaking, which stands firm while the water calms around it.
philosophy.explanation: The emperor-philosopher pictures the steady mind as a rock that stays put while trouble crashes against it.
philosophy.tie_back: His headland and the Kural’s elephant are both images of the strong mind that does not yield in disaster.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong match on steadfastness under assault.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளம் இலாதவர் எய்தார் உலகத்து
வள்ளியம் என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullam ilaadhavar eydhaar ulagaththu
Valliyam ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: Those who lack energy of spirit will never know the proud joy of saying, ‘We are the generous givers of the world’.
kurals.elementary: To share lots of cookies with your friends, you first have to bake them. The Kural says people without energy never get to feel the happy pride of being the one who gives to everyone, because they never make enough to give.
kurals.university: ‘Ullam ilaadhavar’ again uses ullam for ookkam; ‘vallium ennum serukku’ is the elation or proud self-regard (serukku) of being able to say ‘we are liberal’ (valliyam, from vallal, a munificent patron). The logic, drawn out by Parimelazhagar, is that liberality requires wealth, wealth requires effort, and effort requires ookkam, so the unenergetic are cut off from one of the highest satisfactions of kingship and householdership, the role of the vallal celebrated in Sangam poetry (the seven great patrons, kadaiyezhu vallalgal). Solomon Pappaiah calls it ‘mana uyarvu’, uplift of mind, while Kalaignar reads ‘ullam’ as the eager will to give freely. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s reading, ‘pride of having conquered the world’, diverges from the mainstream. Thirukkural.net’s ‘the poor in spirit can never attain the pride of being the generous patrons of the world’ matches the majority view; the Tamil is identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The teacher’s parting instruction to graduating students tells them to give with faith, not without faith, to give with liberality (śriyā), with modesty, with awe and with understanding.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad treats generous giving as a mark of a noble, full-hearted life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural adds that such magnificent giving is only possible for the energetic.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; shares the ideal of liberal giving but does not link it to energy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says true giving flows from a willing, glad heart rather than reluctance.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see generous giving as springing from largeness of heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares heart-driven generosity; the Kural stresses the energy needed to have something to give.

islam.quote_or_event: “The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is that of the giver and the lower (hand) is that of the beggar.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises the dignity of being the one who gives rather than the one who must ask.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise prizes the honour of being a giver, which the unenergetic never attain.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in valuing the giver’s position; it does not mention energy explicitly.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs observes that one person scatters freely and yet grows richer, while another withholds and comes to want, and that the generous soul will be enriched and the one who waters others will himself be watered.
judaism.explanation: The sages praise the open-handed, large-spirited person who gives freely.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Proverbs treats generosity as the mark of a big spirit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; praises generosity but does not tie it to the prior energy that makes giving possible.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that misers do not reach the heavenly realms and fools do not praise generosity, but the wise rejoice in giving and are happy because of it.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha contrasts small-minded misers with the wise, who find joy in giving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly says only the large-spirited taste the joy of generosity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; parallel on joy in giving, but the contrast is miserliness, not lack of energy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon, who had almost nothing, eagerly served disguised Zeus and Hermes their best food and wine when every rich household had turned the gods away.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poorest couple in the district proved the most generous because their hearts were large.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The story shows that the pride of generosity belongs to the large-hearted, as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shows generosity arising from spirit, not wealth, which partly cuts against the Kural’s link between energy, wealth and giving.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle’s great-souled (megalopsychos) person is the sort who confers benefits but is ashamed to receive them, and who likes to repay more than he received.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle’s ideal of greatness of soul includes taking pride in being a benefactor.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s ‘pride of being generous’, which belongs only to those with a large spirit.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; close match to the ‘serukku’ (pride) of the liberal patron.

kurals.tamil:
பரியது கூர்ங்கோட்டது ஆயினும் யானை
வெரூஉம் புலிதாக் குறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pariyadhu koorngottadhu aayinum yaanai
Veruum pulidhaakkurin.
kurals.meaning: Though the elephant is huge and armed with sharp tusks, it takes fright when a tiger attacks.
kurals.elementary: A big dog can run away from a small, brave cat that hisses and charges. The Kural says size and weapons don’t decide who wins; the fierce spirit does, like a tiger that can scare an elephant.
kurals.university: The couplet is a pure illustration (eduththukkaattu uvamai) with the moral left implicit: ‘pariyadhu’ (bulky) and ‘koorng kottadhu’ (having sharp tusks) list the elephant’s physical advantages, and ‘veruum’ (fears) is an alapedai (vowel-lengthened) form of verum, which heightens the sense of sudden fright. Parimelazhagar explains that the tiger prevails because it has ookkam, and that the verse teaches that energy, not bulk or weaponry, decides contests; Kalaignar makes this explicit, calling ookkam stronger than physique. The pairing with 597, where the elephant is the image of steadfastness, shows Valluvar using the same animal both ways: wounded but energetic it stands, huge but unenergetic it flees. The text is identical in the base sources; transliterations differ only in rendering the alapedai (veru-um / veruum).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya records a debate on whether energy (utsāha-śakti) or material power (prabhāva-śakti) is superior: his teacher argues that an energetic king, brave and skilled, can overcome even a stronger one, while Kautilya himself ranks power, and above both good counsel, higher.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra weighs energy against sheer resources as sources of victory.
hinduism.tie_back: The teacher’s view is the Kural’s tiger-and-elephant lesson; Kautilya’s own view is a candid counterpoint.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Directly on topic, but Kautilya’s final ranking differs from the Kural’s, and the paraphrase is from memory of the Shamasastry translation.

christianity.quote_or_event: The young shepherd David, without armour and armed only with a sling, faces the giant Philistine champion Goliath, clad in bronze with a massive spear, and fells him with one stone.
christianity.explanation: The small but fearless fighter overcomes the huge, heavily armed one.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s tiger, David shows that spirit beats size and weapons.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear narrative parallel; the Bible credits the victory to faith in God as much as courage.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Before facing Goliath’s army, Saul’s few steadfast soldiers declare that small, determined forces often defeat larger ones.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s tiger-versus-elephant lesson applied to armies.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on the few overcoming the many; victory is attributed to God’s permission and patience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be strong as a leopard, and swift as an eagle, and fleet as a gazelle, and brave as a lion, to do the will of your Father who is in heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Judah ben Tema calls for the fierce energy of predators in the service of God.
judaism.tie_back: His leopard and lion are the Jewish counterpart of the Kural’s tiger, symbols of energetic spirit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares big-cat imagery of zeal, but lacks the Kural’s contrast with a larger, frightened opponent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Heedful among the heedless, wide-awake among the sleepy, the wise man advances like a swift horse leaving behind a weak jade.”
buddhism.explanation: The alert, energetic person pulls far ahead of those who are sluggish.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it teaches that alert energy, not bulk, decides who prevails.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Contrasts energy with sluggishness, but lacks the size-versus-spirit contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the cave of the giant Cyclops Polyphemus, the far smaller Odysseus blinds him with a sharpened stake and escapes with his men under the giant’s sheep.
greek_mythology.explanation: The small but bold hero overcomes a monstrous opponent many times his size.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode matches the Kural’s point that bulk does not guarantee victory over a spirited foe.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Victory comes as much from cunning as from energy, so the fit is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Rallying the Greek officers after their generals had been seized by the Persians, Xenophon tells them that it is neither numbers nor strength that wins victories in war: whichever side advances with the stronger spirit, its enemies as a rule will not stand against it.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon urges the officers to restore the courage of their troops, since morale, not size, decides battles.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the tiger routing the huge, tusked elephant, the side with the stronger spirit prevails over sheer bulk.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Anabasis, Book III, ch. 1, §42 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Book III text could not be loaded this session to verify wording, so no quotation is given. Strong match on spirit outweighing size and strength; Xenophon speaks of armies, not single animals.

kurals.tamil:
உரமொருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கைஅஃ தில்லார்
மரம்மக்க ளாதலே வேறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Uram oruvarku ulla verukkai aqdhillaar
Maram makkal aadhale veru.
kurals.meaning: A person’s real strength is abundance of inner energy; those without it are trees, differing from them only in having human shape.
kurals.elementary: A tree stands in one place all day and never tries anything new. The Kural says a person with no energy or drive is like a tree that happens to look like a human. What makes us truly alive is our eagerness to act.
kurals.university: ‘Uram’ is strength or firmness, and ‘ulla verukkai’ is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes verukkai as abundance, hence ‘excess of ookkam is one’s strength’, while others take verukkai in its lexical sense of wealth (selvam), hence ‘energy is the mind’s wealth’, which is Pope’s ‘energy is mental wealth’. Solomon Pappaiah glosses uram as thinniya arivu (firm understanding). The second line’s ‘maram makkal aadhale veru’ is devastating: the only difference (veru) between the energy-less and trees is that they have become human in form. Parimelazhagar notes the chapter closes by returning to 591, where the energy-less were denied possession; here they are denied full humanity. The text is identical in the base sources; the sandhi form ‘verukkaiaqdhillaar’ contains the aaydham (ஃ) of ‘aqdhu’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Queen Vidula rebukes her son Sanjaya, who lies despondent after defeat, telling him it is better to blaze up for a moment than to smoulder for a long time, and urging him to rise and fight.
hinduism.explanation: A mother shames her listless son, saying a life without energy is not worth living.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidula’s contempt for smouldering inertia matches the Kural’s picture of the energy-less as mere trees.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 133-136 (Vidula’s counsel), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; one of the closest Indian parallels to this chapter’s theme.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;”
christianity.explanation: Paul lists fervour of spirit and freedom from sloth as marks of Christian life.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see spiritual energy as essential and sluggishness as a failure of real life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Positive exhortation to zeal; lacks the Kural’s harsh tree comparison.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up…”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the hypocrites look impressive but are hollow inside, like timber propped against a wall.
islam.tie_back: The Kural uses the same wood image for people with human form but no inner life of energy.
islam._accuracy_note: Striking shared image of humans as lifeless wood; the Qur’an’s target is hypocrisy, not lack of energy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel urges people to step up with energy and responsibility when others do nothing.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats being fully human as a matter of active striving, not mere form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that true humanity is earned through effort; the context is moral leadership.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day strenuous and resolute than to live a hundred years sluggish and dissipated.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada values a single day of energetic life above a century of lazy existence.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that life without energy is hardly life at all.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in judgement on the worth of an energy-less life.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says both gods and men are angry with the man who lives idle, for he is like the stingless drones that waste the bees’ labour, eating without working.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod compares the idle to drones in a hive, living beings that contribute nothing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s drone and the Kural’s tree are both images of life without energy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; archaic Greek didactic poetry rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle, seeking the distinctive human function, sets aside mere life because it is shared even with plants, and locates the human good in the active exercise of the rational soul.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, a person who only lives and grows is functioning at the level of a plant, not yet as a human being.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own claim: without active energy, humans are trees in human shape.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a remarkably close parallel that even uses the plant comparison.
